title: LLVMhammer turns a DRAM bit flip into persistent LLM inference slowdown
dek: A Rowhammer-induced compiler fault yields correct but slower cached Triton GPU kernels across vendors.
evidence: Primary academic preprint; experimental threat model requires exploitable CPU DRAM faults
takeaway: Include compiled-kernel integrity and performance anomalies in inference supply-chain threat models.

sections.title: Mechanism

bullets.detail: The attack flips a bit in Triton's CPU-side MLIR/LLVM optimization pipeline, producing a functionally correct but suboptimal GPU kernel.
Triton caches generated kernels to disk. After the corruption, later inference runs can inherit the slowdown even when the bit-flip is no longer active.

paragraphs: Target: The attack flips a bit in Triton's CPU-side MLIR/LLVM optimization pipeline, producing a functionally correct but suboptimal GPU kernel.
Persistence: Triton caches generated kernels to disk. After the corruption, later inference runs can inherit the slowdown even when the bit-flip is no longer active.

sections.title: Evidence and defense

bullets.detail: Across four open models on NVIDIA RTX 4090 and AMD RX 7900 XTX, the paper reports 4–16% server inference-latency increases; separate tests explore output corruption.

The paper demonstrates a physical-memory fault scenario rather than a typical remote prompt-injection pathway. Treat unusual kernel-cache changes, binary provenance and sustained latency regression as potential indicators.
